metadata.label: Pub Note
metadata.value: This 12 cm thick volume has a regular title page, handwritten table of contents, and introductory 42 page text in Gothic German. The decorative title page and maps are in Latin or German. Maps hand colored and lavishly illustrated. "Johann Babtiste Homann (1664-1724), Nuremberg, was born in Oberkammlach, the Electorate of Bavaria. Although educated at a Jesuit school, and preparing for an ecclesiastical career, he eventually converted to Protestantism and from 1687 worked as a civil law notary in Nuremberg. He soon turned to engraving and cartography; in 1702 he founded his own publishing house. Homann acquired renown as a leading German cartographer, and in 1715 was appointed Imperial Geographer by Emperor Charles VI." (Adina Sommer, Antique and Contemporary Art, Munich). This is an early edition of his world atlas, with many maps added later by an owner and with the index pages in manuscript - indicating that this was a composite version of Homann's world atlas, made up for the customer. Publication date is estimated at 1716 from the title page, but most of the maps are undated.

metadata.label: Pub Note
metadata.value: "A stunning 1839 - 1859 set of 7 Sigismond Visconti astronomical charts issued by Auguste-Henri Dufour and Charles Simonneau. The charts represent the summation of astronomical knowledge regarding the Solar System and the orbits of the earth and moon, as understood in the early 19th century. The set consist of seven plates, which are as follows: The Solar System - Centered on the sun, displays the entire solar system as far as Neptune. Includes the asteroid belt objects Vesta, Junon, Ceres and Pallas. Identifies moos surrounding Earth, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune. A comet, possibly Halley's, is also identified. Dated 1859. Revised by Dufour to reflect the 1846 discovery of Neptune. Orbit of the Earth - Details the orbit of the Earth around the sun, showing the axis of the Earth and the solar effects on the seasons. Equinox and solstice points are noted. Planisphere - Added to the Visconti set by Dufour in 1830. Illustrates the position of the Earth relative to the Sun in each month of the year. Four seasons are futher identified in each corner. So too are the signs of the zodiac. Dated 1839. Phases of the Moon - This chart illustrates the phases of the moon relative to the Earth and Sun. Dated 1839. Flux and Reflux - Attempts to illustrate the effect of the Sun and moon on the Tides relative to the rotation of the Earth and Moon. Dated 1839. Eclipses of the Sun and Moon - Illustrates the positions of the Sun and moon during full and partial solar and lunar eclipses. Dated 1839. Cross-section of the Earth - Illustrates the earth and its atmosphere as a cross-section. Radiating bands of shading illustrate the layers of the Earth. The volcanoes Pichincha in Columbia and Mount Ophir in Sumatra are noted. Also noted are the Galapagos Islands, South America, Africa, San Tome, the Maluku Islands, and the Isle of Dundas (British Columbia). Each chart features explicative text at its base. Publication History and Census This set, minus the planisphere (plate 3) was originally engraved A. Gianni and published by Sigismund Visconti in 1815. A second and third edition issued by Chez Vilquin of the 6 astronomical plates appeared in 1820. Auguste-Henri Dufour and Charles Simonneau published a revised third edition, adding plate no. 3, the planisphere, in 1830, renumbering the remaining plates. A fourth edition, also by Dufour and Simonneau appeared in 1839, and a fifth in 1859. The preset sent appears to be a composite, with the first plate being from the 1859 edition, and the remaining plates form the 1839 edition. All editions and examples are rare on the market, especially representing a complete set. Sigismond Visconti (November 13, 1785 - 18??) was an Italian-French writer and scholar active in Paris during the early 19th century. Visconti was born in Rome. He is best known for his 1815 publication of a series of astronomical engravings illustrating the solar system as it was understood in the early 19th century. Adolphe Hippolyte Dufour (1795 - 1865), also known as Auguste-Henri Dufour, was a Paris based map and atlas publisher active in the middle to late 19th century. Dufour claimed to be a student of another French cartographer, Emile Lapie. He is known to have worked with numerous other French cartographers, publishers, and engravers of the period including Andriveau-Goujon, Charles Dyonnet, and Duvotenay. His corpus includes numerous maps and atlases, the most striking of which is probably his monumental elephant folio Atlas Universel Physique, Historique et Politique Geographie Ancienne et Moderne. Dufour's student and successor was Alexandre Vuillemin." (Geographicus, 2022)

metadata.label: Pub Note
metadata.value: "Inscribed to the reverse of the front end paper: "To Sir James & Lady Baird from Anne E. Nasmyth in remembrance of her dear husband James Nasmyth who died on the 9th of May 1890 in his 82nd year. Hammerfield Kent". Anne Nasmyth (nee Hartop, b. 1817 d. 1893) was a notable artist, specialising in botanical studies, who married James Nasmyth in 1840. The recipients were Sir James Gardiner Baird, 7th Baronet (1813-1896) and Lady Henrietta Mary Baird (nee Wauchope). An important title, both in the history of astronomy for its remarkably detailed depictions of the lunar surface(achieved by painstakingly constructing plaster models from numerous observations and then photographing them), and as an early photographically illustrated book, which utilised a number of different methods of reproducing the images, including heliotypes and Woodburytypes. This is an interesting and poignant association copy, presumably Anne Nasmyth's own prior to presenting it to the Bairds." (Frost, 2022) "Nasmyth was brought up in an artistic family, made a fortune as a manufacturer and inventor, and retired to take up astronomy. He built his own 20" reflector in 1842 (inventing the Nasmyth focus in the process), and began to concentrate on lunar studies. Nasmyth brought photography to the aid of selenography in an unusual manner. Since photography was not yet advanced enough to take photographs of lunar details, Nasmyth constructed plaster models based on visual observations, and then photographed the models. For this book, the photographs were then printed by the arduous Woodburytype process, perhaps the most faithful method ever devised for the reproduction of photographs. The Woodburytype has no grain whatsoever, because it does not use cracks or dots to reproduce tone. Instead, a relief mold is made of the image in lead, so that the areas of dark tone are deep and light tone shallow. Ink suspended in gelatin is cast in the mold, and the resulting print produces contrast by the thickness or thinness of the ink." (Linda Hall Library, Face of the Moon 20). "Nasmyth’s simulated views of the moon supported his specious claim that the craggy pockmarked lunar surface was the result of volcanic activity. Rather than declaring Nasmyth’s methodology unscientific, however, his contemporaries lauded the visual effects and found his arguments convincing. This reception suggests that the photographic medium itself imbued the images with a sense of veracity that lent them scientific authority." (Metropolitan Museum)

metadata.label: Note
metadata.value: First edition of the lunar atlas with drawings of 25 areas of the Moon on 20 lithographed plates in the printed beige paper cover case, by Fauth the lunar cartographer who relied principally on visual observations. His Lunar topographical formations were superb, both in their representation and accuracy, and he quickly became well respected in astronomical circles. The present, early atlas dates from Fauth's period at a private observatory at Kaiserslautern. The correct number of plates is 20, as numbered XXI, plate XII was never published (as per contents sheet: 'fehlt'). Inside front cover: Zu gefl. Beachtung. Includes hachures to indicate the length and steepness of the slopes of the various features.

metadata.label: Pub Note
metadata.value: Reduced-format edition, reproducing at two-fifths scale the celebrated photographic enlargements by Loewy and Puiseux from their Atlas Lunaire. Title, 71 plates, plus 3 additional plates. Issued in 12 parts. 71 photographic plates printed by half-tone from the original lunar heliogravure photographs, each with printed tissue overlays. Extra-illustrated with three smaller heliogravure plates (approx. 25 × 18 cm) of the entire Moon by Fillon & Heuse after Loewy and Puiseux, captioned “Lunar photograph obtained at the Paris Observatory” and Lunar Atlas Plates A–C, and with a later map of lunar craters. Later half-cloth, preserving original printed wrappers from one part (boards bowed). Condition: some headlines shaved by the binder, a few plates lightly creased, occasional light wear or light soiling; one plate (XXIX) lacking its printed overlay and instead supplied with a contemporary pen-and-ink annotated overlay, likely original to the issue. The rare reduced-format edition of Loewy and Puiseux’s Atlas Lunaire, issued by the Société Belge d’Astronomie for its members and never sold commercially. Published in fascicules concurrently with the monumental large-format edition produced by the Imprimerie Nationale between 1896 and 1910, this version reproduced all 71 plates at a more portable scale for use by amateur and professional astronomers alike. As stated in the Bulletin of the Belgian Astronomical Society (1897–1898), the atlas was intended as both a practical vade mecum for lunar observation and a precise scientific reference; members could purchase individual issues for 5 francs. With Society membership numbering only 200–400, and not all members subscribing, the print run was necessarily small. Loewy, director of the Paris Observatory, and Puiseux devoted over fourteen years to the project, working under the severe constraints of atmospheric conditions: only 50–60 suitable nights per year, yielding just four or five usable negatives. In total, nearly six thousand photographs were taken over some five hundred evenings. The resulting atlas has been described as “the ultimate achievement of nineteenth-century astronomical photography” (The Photobook), and remained the standard photographic map of the Moon until the advent of space probes in the 1960s; images of substantially higher quality were not obtained until the 1970s. Rare: ABPC and AE record no copies at auction. WorldCat lists mostly incomplete examples, typically with 35–53 plates. As with the large-format edition, this reduced edition was complete at 71 plates; copies are frequently encountered without text, perhaps as issued. Cf. The Photobook, vol. I, pp. 54–55 (first edition).

metadata.label: Pub Note
metadata.value: Un site lunaire : (Le Palus Putredinis), by J. Deseilligny. Published by the Société Anonyme Notre-Dame des Anges in Autun (Saône-et-Loire), France, 1905. Lunar atlas comprised of a “Journal” volume, followed by three volumes of plates: Planches I, II and III. Title translates to: A Lunar Site: (the Palus Putredinis). Four-volume set housed together within a five-sided box covered in dark green linen with tan paper wrapping, printed with title, authorship and brief description of contents: 1re Série. Journal et Planches [= 1st Series. Journal and Boards]. Interior lined with marbled paper and includes a brown ribbon for securing volumes in place. Each volume bound in dark green linen-covered board with tan paper wrapping, printed with title, authorship and brief description of contents, e.g.: 1re Série. Journal [= 1st Series. Journal]. Tan paper labels on each spine, e.g.: 1st Series. Journal -- MCMV [1905]. Marbled end papers in each volume. Pages are sewn into binding of Journal; leaves of plates in Planches I-III are hole-punched and bound together with green cord. Plates in all volumes are mounted onto sheets. Journal collation: [8] pages, [1] leaf of plates, [1], 2-240, [4] pages (first and last two pages are blank). Includes title page, dedication, introduction, one lunar map on leaf of plates, three lunar diagrams appearing within the text on pages 54-55, 60-61 and 162-163, Appendices A, B and C, table of contents and colophon. Imprint for entire work presented on colophon of Journal. (All text pages viewable here as a composite image.) Planches I: [2] leaves, I-III, III (bis), IV-XLII leaves of plates, [2] leaves (first and last two leaves are blank). Includes 45 maps on 43 leaves of plates. Planches II: [2] leaves, XLIII-LXXXIV leaves of plates, [2] leaves (first and last two leaves are blank). Includes 42 maps on 42 leaves of plates. Planches III: [2] leaves, LXXXV-CXXV leaves of plates, [2] leaves (first and last two leaves are blank). Includes 40 maps and one view on 41 leaves of plates. Planches III has Appendices B and C but no A. Each volume has an ink signature - on title page of Journal and first blank page of Planches I, II and III. In total, atlas contains 3 lunar diagrams, 128 lunar maps and one view of a telescope. Black and white illustrations make up the first 125 lunar maps, and photographs the last three, as well as the view. Maps show topography, including craters. Relief shown pictorially and through shading. Date and hours of observations noted both alongside imagery and in lower margin of each sheet. Some maps provide insets, which present outline versions of the main map, indexed. Some of the main maps are also indexed, and a few contain question marks throughout. Illustrations focus on the area of Le Palus Putredinis [= Palus Putredinis]. Photographs present the moon in partial view, half-view and three-quarter-view, showing stunning details of the craters and other lunar features. All together a beautiful early synthesis of art and science on the moon. The Palus Putredinis - "Marsh of Decay" - is a lunar swamp. The area “stretches from the crater Archimedes southeast toward the rugged Montes Apenninus range located on the southeastern edge of Mare Imbrium. In the southern part of this area is a rille system designated Rimae Archimedes. To the south is a prominent linear rille named Rima Bradley, and to the east is the Rima Hadley, which served as the landing site for Apollo 15, and the Rimae Fresnel” (see link in Pub Reference for further information). "First edition, exceptionally rare, and presentation copy (see below) of this highly detailed topographic study of Palus Putredinus (the ‘Marsh of Decay’), a vast lava field within the Mare Imbrium on the surface of the moon, and containing the landing site of Apollo 15. The 126 plates comprise 122 photographs of detailed drawings of sectors of the Sea, executed by Jules Alfred Pierrot Deseilligny (1868–1918), amateur astronomer, founder of the French Society of Selenography, and a friend of Camille Flammarion. These drawings were based on Deseilligny’s observations made with his own telescope. A further three photographs were taken at the Paris Observatory, and a further one through Deseilligny’s telescope. This largely unknown work appears to be the most detailed study of an area of the moon up to the time of its publication. It is not in the Linda Hall catalogue The face of the moon, not mentioned in Whitaker’s Mapping and naming the moon, nor in Sheehan and Dobbins’ Epic moon. A history of lunar exploration in the age of the telescope. OCLC records only Harvard. Deseilligny devoted himself to selenography. He founded the Commission lunaire, an association of French astronomers, of which he was the first president. In 1906 they published the Projet d'etudes selenographiques en commun. (This work is) probably the rarest work on lunar topography known. It is also fascinating that at the time, drawing was considered more capable of rendering an accurate depiction of surface features than photography, so you have photographs of drawings (and in other works of the time, drawn highlights on photographs). Whereas at the same time Lowell was making drawings of things he thought he saw, and then photographing the results. The same approach but with very different outcomes. Provenance: The colophon of the first volume states: ‘Etude faite pour La Societe Astronomique de France. Exemplaire tire specialement pour Monsieur Loewy’, below which is a handwritten dedication by the author ‘en homage respecteuse de l’lauteur J. Deseilligny’. This is a dedication to the astronomer Maurice Loewy (1833–1907). Loewy was born on April 15, 1833 in Marianske Lazne, in what is now the Czech Republic. Lowey moved to Vienna in 1841 to become an assistant at the Vienna Observatory, working on celestial mechanics. In 1860, the director of the Observatory, Karl L. Littrow, secured a position for Lowey under Urbain Le Verrier, the director of the Paris Observatory. There he worked on the orbits of asteroids and comets and on the measurement of longitude, improving the accuracy of the Connaissance des Temps. He was elected a member of the Bureau des Longitudes in 1872 and of the Academie des Sciences in 1873. In 1896, Loewy became the director of the Paris Observatory. He is mainly known through his work on astrophotography with Pierre Henri Puiseux. " (William P. Watson, 2020).

metadata.label: Pub Note
metadata.value: "This large, richly illustrated folding map–game is a singular example of mid-20th-century French graphic culture, combining cartography, literature, and playful philosophy into a coherent visual cosmology. Drawn to promote the Jura wines of Henri Maire, the image is a rich blend of science fiction, lunar map and cleverly interwoven vignettes celebrating 12 celebrated writers/poets from the preceding three millenia. The central image is the work of celebrated French animator Paul Grimault, who in 1947 created France's first feature-length animated film and is respected worldwide as one of France's greatest animators of the 20th century, with the title and conceit doubling as an homage to famed French fimmaker Georges Méliès (1861–1938). Conceived as both a board game and a poetic atlas, Voyage Fantastique dans La Lune invites the viewer to traverse an imagined lunar world structured as a circular landscape, its paths and regions corresponding to twelve “anthologies lunaires,” each governed by a poet drawn from classical antiquity through the modern era. The work belongs to a brief but fertile moment when commercial ephemera embraced ambitious intellectual and artistic programs rather than mere advertising. Paul Grimault’s contribution is central. Best known for his work in animation and for Le Roi et l’Oiseau, Grimault here translates cinematic imagination into static form, orchestrating a continuous lunar panorama populated with symbolic landscapes, mythological references, and narrative vignettes. The composition reads simultaneously as a map, a dream sequence, and a moral allegory. Pathways function as a “fil d’Ariane,” guiding the participant through successive poetic realms, while the circular format evokes both the lunar globe and the cyclical nature of literary tradition. The Twelve Poets of the Lunar Anthologies At the intellectual core of the game are the twelve poets whose texts, fragments, and imagined “experiences” structure the journey. Each poet represents not merely an author but an entire cultural moment, condensed into symbolic episodes scored by points. The selection deliberately spans civilizations and centuries, suggesting a universal, transhistorical republic of poetry. Homer (traditionally dated to the 8th century BCE) anchors the sequence in mythic antiquity. His lunar domain evokes epic origins: Babylon, Lesbos, Carthage, and the courts of Solomon and the Queen of Sheba, situating Homer as the primal source of narrative imagination. Aristophanes (c. 445–386 BCE) represents Old Comedy, satire, and civic wit. His scenes—Delos, Delphi, Aspasia, Socrates—foreground irony, political intelligence, and the theatrical spirit of classical Athens. Virgil (70–19 BCE) embodies Roman order and moral gravity. The options attributed to him—Cleopatra and Caesar, Apicius, Vercingetorix, Cicero—reflect Rome’s synthesis of power, rhetoric, and spectacle. Longus (dates uncertain, 2nd–5th century) introduces pastoral romance. His association with Daphnis and Chloe emphasizes innocence, nature, and lyrical eros as a counterpoint to epic and satire. Li Bai (701–762), presented in French as Li Pai, brings Chinese lyricism and intoxicated transcendence. His lunar scenes—Scheherazade, Harun al-Rashid, Charlemagne—blend Eastern poetry with Western fantasy, underscoring the game’s universalist ambitions. Omar Khayyam (1048–1131) occupies a philosophical middle ground. His quatrains, steeped in wine, fate, and skepticism, are mirrored in scenes of crusades, medieval Europe, and Constantinople, where contemplation and action collide. Jean Bodel (c. 1165–1210) represents the trouvère tradition. His episodes—saint Louis, Gothic cathedrals, Marco Polo—celebrate medieval narrative, faith, and architectural aspiration. Raoul Ponchon (1848–1937) embodies Belle Époque bohemia. Maxim’s, Monet, Degas, Santos-Dumont, and Méliès situate him in modern Paris, bridging poetry, science, and spectacle. Alfred de Musset (1810–1857) personifies Romantic introspection and love. Venice, George Sand, Beethoven, and Schubert form a melancholy, musical landscape of emotion and artistic struggle. André Chénier (1762–1794) stands at the threshold of revolution. His scenes—Tahiti, Mozart, Catherine II, the Bastille, young Bonaparte—reflect Enlightenment optimism shadowed by political violence. Saint-Amant (1594–1661) contributes Baroque sensuality and courtly excess. Gabrielle d’Estrées, royal hunts, Velázquez, and Bruegel evoke spectacle, power, and artistic abundance. Jean de La Fontaine (1621–1695) closes the cycle with moral clarity and irony. Versailles, Molière, Descartes, and Christina of Sweden frame a reflective conclusion grounded in wit and philosophical distance. Printed by the prestigious Imprimerie Oberthur in 1959, the map reflects postwar France’s renewed confidence in culture as a unifying force. While ostensibly a promotional object for Jura wines, its ambition far exceeds commercial necessity. The elaborate literary apparatus, the scholarly breadth of its references, and Grimault’s sustained visual invention position it closer to an artist’s book or a didactic fantasy map than to advertising ephemera. As an object, Voyage Fantastique dans La Lune occupies a rare intersection of graphic art, literary history, and imaginative cartography. It is both playful and erudite, inviting slow reading as much as visual exploration. In reconstructing a “paradis perdu” of poetry across forty centuries, Grimault and his collaborators produced not merely a game, but a coherent lunar world, one that stands as a testament to the enduring power of poetry to map the invisible territories of human experience. Georges Méliès (1861–1938) The game is also a noteworthy tribute to the early French filmmaker Georges Méliès, and even names him explicitly as one of the “Raoul Ponchon” episodes: “Aider Méliès dans une scène de son film: Le Voyage dans la lune.” This work is consciously aligned with the tradition of French lunar fantasy inaugurated by Méliès, particularly Le Voyage dans la lune (1902), whose episodic structure and theatrical logic provide an implicit model. Like Méliès’s film, Voyage fantastique dans la lune rejects scientific realism in favor of a deliberately constructed, poetic moon; a stage upon which a succession of self-contained scenes unfolds. Méliès’s cinema advanced by tableaux, each vignette presenting a new marvel, encounter, or transformation; Grimault’s map–game operates on the same principle, guiding the participant through discrete “anthologies” that function as literary and visual set-pieces rather than geographic destinations. The explicit invitation to “help Méliès in a scene of his film” confirms this lineage, positioning the work not as parody but as homage. In translating Méliès’s cinematic fantasy into graphic form, Grimault extends early twentieth-century illusionistic cinema into mid-century printed culture, preserving the moon as a privileged site of imagination where spectacle, memory, and artifice supersede exploration. The poster map is extremely rare. We were unable to locate any other examples. We do note that Grimault created other artwork for Henri Maire's Vin Fou. Paul Grimault (23 March 1905 – 29 March 1994) was one of the most important figures in the history of French animation. Working almost exclusively in traditional hand-drawn animation, Grimault developed a visual language that stood apart from both American studio animation and contemporary European experiments, favoring poetic ambiguity, political nuance, and expressive restraint. His films often blend fantasy with quiet social commentary, aligning animation with literary and artistic traditions rather than purely commercial entertainment. Grimault’s career was decisively shaped by the founding of the studio Les Gémeaux in 1936, which he established with producer André Sarrut. This venture marked the revival of serious French animation after the earlier pioneering work of Émile Cohl. During the Second World War, when American animated films were largely unavailable in France, Les Gémeaux found a receptive audience and produced a series of short films that demonstrated Grimault’s growing artistic confidence. However, the studio overextended itself with La Bergère et le Ramoneur (1948), intended as the first French feature-length animated film, and closed in 1952 following the financial and artistic turmoil surrounding that project. The troubled history of La Bergère et le Ramoneur ultimately gave rise to Grimault’s masterpiece, Le Roi et l’oiseau. Begun in 1948 with a screenplay by Jacques Prévert, the film was prematurely shown in an unfinished form in 1952 against Grimault’s wishes, leading to a rupture with Sarrut and a halt in production. Only in 1967 did Grimault regain control of the material, allowing him to resume work with both original collaborators and a younger generation of animators. Completed and released in 1980 under its final title, Le Roi et l’oiseau is now regarded as a cornerstone of European animation, widely admired for its visual sophistication, political allegory, and enduring influence. Alongside this monumental project, Grimault produced a substantial body of short films, many of which he later gathered into the retrospective feature La Table tournante (1988), made in collaboration with Jacques Demy. His work extended beyond cinema into advertising, live-action hybrids, and television, while his early involvement with the agitprop Groupe Octobre introduced him to Jacques Prévert, whose collaboration proved central to Grimault’s artistic identity. By the end of his life, Grimault was widely recognized as a formative influence on later animators in France and beyond, having demonstrated that animation could sustain poetic depth, intellectual ambition, and formal elegance over an entire career." (Ruderman, 2026)

metadata.label: Pub Note
metadata.value: The Photographic lunar atlas was published in 1960 by The University of Chicago Press. It is accompanied by a text booklet, which includes metrics: The main body of the Atlas has 184 [i.e. 188] sheets containing 212 photographs; the Introduction contains 11 sheets with 5 photographs, the Supplements 35 sheets with 63 photographs. The totals are therefore 230 [i.e. 234] sheets and 281 [i.e. 280] photographs. Of these, 94 are from Mount Wilson [Los Angeles, California]; 63, Lick [Mt. Hamilton, California]; 52, McDonald [Fort Davis, Texas]; 41, Yerkes [Williams Bay, Wisconsin]; and 31, Pic du Midi [Bagnères-de-Bigorre, France]. Housed within a box enclosure, these photographs appear in alphabetized sets separated by tabs, beginning with the Introduction, which includes Photographs and Charts 1-11, and followed by: A2-A7 (each numbered set includes parts a-d), B1-B8 (a-d), C1 (a-f), C2-C7 (a-f), C8 (a-f), D1 (a-f), D2-D7 (a-d), D8 (a-f), E1-E8 (a-d), F2-F7 (a-d), and S1-S35. (Lacks sets A1 and F1.) According to the Introduction of the Photographic lunar atlas: "The purpose of this Atlas is to present the surface record of the moon as shown on the best photographs now available." Two supplemental volumes were published subsequently: the Orthographic atlas of the moon : Supplement one in 1961 by the University of Arizona Press (see Pub List No. 14058.000), and the Rectified lunar atlas : Supplement two in 1963, by the Aeronautical Chart and Information Center, United States Air Force (see Pub List No. 14059.000). In the Orthographic atlas of the moon, "the most representative photographs of each of the 44 fields or provinces into which the visible lunar surface was divided in the Photographic lunar atlas are reproduced, supplied with the standard orthographic grid ... " (Introduction). The Rectified lunar atlas contains "a series of high-quality photographs of the lunar surface as it would appear if viewed from above" (Introduction). Note on terminology: photographs and charts are differentiated here as follows - photographs are the original representations of the moon, in black and white, and without the overlay of interpretive graphics and text; charts are those same base images, in blue and white, mediated by overlaid interpretive graphics and text. One could even consider the photographs as art and the charts as maps.
